claims.claim: Hobb, quoted by the reporter, reads Keffria Vestrit's ceding of decisions to her husband as a rule about power: power not exercised is lost.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, quoted by Pauline Bock, New Statesman, 27 July 2018
claims.quote: if you do not exercise your power, it goes away
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'The Elderlings books never ignore women’s stories'

claims.claim: Hobb says setting is a third element the fantasy writer must supply that mainstream writers need not, contrasting a 1970s Chevrolet, which arrives with its own impact, against a horse and cart whose condition she must establish with detail.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Rebecca Lovatt, The Arched Doorway, 24 November 2014 (transcript)
claims.quote: put in enough detail that the reader picks that up
claims.page: answer to the question on the fantasy genre expanding

claims.claim: Hobb says she admires the fantasy writers of the earlier paperback generation because every sentence in their work carries character development, setting and plot at once.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Rebecca Lovatt, The Arched Doorway, 24 November 2014 (transcript)
claims.quote: every sentence is freighted with character development, and setting, and plot
claims.page: answer to the question on the fantasy genre expanding

claims.claim: Hobb reports the physical constraint she wrote under early on: she was told a paperback binding would not hold more than 250 pages, and had to tell her story within that number of words and pages.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Rebecca Lovatt, The Arched Doorway, 24 November 2014 (transcript)
claims.quote: a paperback binding would not hold more than 250 pages
claims.page: answer to the question on the fantasy genre expanding

claims.claim: Hobb states the limit of her preferred first person as a rule of disclosure: the narration can tell the reader exactly what the hero knows and no more.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Rebecca Lovatt, The Arched Doorway, 24 November 2014 (transcript)
claims.quote: you can only tell the reader exactly what the hero knows
claims.page: answer to 'how do you decide whether a story should be told in first or third-person?'

claims.claim: Hobb describes her third-person practice as a very tight point of view in which any given scene stays inside one character only, never switching mid-conversation.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Rebecca Lovatt, The Arched Doorway, 24 November 2014 (transcript)
claims.quote: in any given scene, you will only be with one character
claims.page: answer to 'how do you decide whether a story should be told in first or third-person?'

claims.claim: Hobb calls first person the most intimate voice and likens it to the voice a family uses in the evening or a mother recounting her childhood.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Rebecca Lovatt, The Arched Doorway, 24 November 2014 (transcript)
claims.quote: It is the most intimate voice
claims.page: answer to 'how do you decide whether a story should be told in first or third-person?'

claims.claim: Hobb says that fantasy full of pratfalls and silliness is fun but lessens the impact felt when a character is hurt or disappointed.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Rebecca Lovatt, The Arched Doorway, 24 November 2014 (transcript)
claims.quote: it lessens the impact that you feel if the character is hurt

claims.claim: Hobb says she planted clues at the end of the Tawny Man trilogy that only readers attending to every detail of the book would have picked up as signalling more story to come.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Rebecca Lovatt, The Arched Doorway, 24 November 2014 (transcript)
claims.quote: readers who were really reading every detail of the book
claims.page: answer to 'Did you know you’d be coming back all these years later'

claims.claim: Reviewer Lew Kelly charges Hobb with an overreliance on adverbs in Ship of Magic, saying it stunts the novel's flow.
claims.quote: Her overreliance on adverbs often stunts the novel’s flow
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'The opening of the novel'

claims.claim: Kelly describes The Mad Ship as tracking a household and a city together: as the Vestrits' domestic situation worsens, so does the political situation in Bingtown.
claims.quote: As their domestic situation worsens, so does the political situation

claims.claim: Kelly names morality as the trilogy's major theme and states its recurring form as a household choice between the morally correct action and the profitable one.
claims.quote: a choice between a morally correct action or a profitable one
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Hobb’s major theme in the trilogy is morality'

claims.claim: Kelly argues Hobb's prose is at its best inside a single character's head, and that the many shifting Liveship viewpoints leave the characters feeling distanced and harder to empathise with.
claims.quote: her talent truly shines when she’s deep inside a characters head
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'The opening of the novel'

claims.claim: The reviewer credits Hobb with conveying a great deal of historical, societal and environmental information through characters who each know different aspects of the same events, without it sounding explanatory.
claims.source: HearWriteNow blog review of The Liveship Traders

claims.claim: The reviewer notes that the Liveship Traders trilogy keeps its multiple viewpoints professionally contained to one viewpoint per scene.
claims.source: HearWriteNow blog review of The Liveship Traders
claims.quote: professionally contained to one viewpoint per scene

verdicts.trueWording: sometimes, like Keffria Vestrit, “if you do not exercise your power, it goes away”, Hobb says
verdicts.note: Live newstatesman.com returned 403 to both plain and browser-UA curl; reached via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20260212161207id_/<url> (200, full article body). Quote exact. Both limbs on the page in the 'The Elderlings books never ignore women’s stories' paragraph: Keffria 'has married a man whom she has let control her life: “She has said: ‘I will let my husband make the decisions, it is easier.’ And so you get an imbalance”', then the power rule attributed to Hobb, and extended by her to not voting.

verdicts.trueWording: setting — “this third element which mainstream writers don’t really have to deal with”
verdicts.note: Live archeddoorway.com returned 403; reached via Wayback raw capture 20240521165048id_ (200, full transcript). Quote exact. Every limb present in the answer on the genre expanding: 'you also have setting – it’s like this third element which mainstream writers don’t really have to deal with. If they say it’s a 1970s Chevrolet, that immediately comes to you with a whole lot of impact. Whereas if I want to describe that the horse and cart that they picked up is not going to get too far, I need to put in enough detail that the reader picks that up.'

verdicts.trueWording: “I really admire the fantasy writers of the generation who wrote to that length”
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture of the Arched Doorway transcript. Quote exact: '...told such amazing stories where every sentence is freighted with character development, and setting, and plot all-in-one.' 'Earlier paperback generation' is the page’s own referent — the generation writing to the 250-page paperback length described two sentences earlier — so the limb is supported, though the phrase 'paperback generation' is the claim’s wording.

verdicts.trueWording: “I was told that a paperback binding would not hold more than 250 pages”
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture. Quote exact, and the second limb follows immediately: 'no matter how much I might want to expand my story, I had to be able to tell it in that number of words and pages.' She also frames herself as 'like the Beatles’ song — a paperback writer.'

verdicts.trueWording: “The limits are, of course, that you can only tell the reader exactly what the hero knows”
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture, answer to 'how do you decide whether a story should be told in first or third-person?'. Quote exact and stated by Hobb explicitly as the limit of her preferred first person ('I always prefer the first-person, if it can be told that way').

verdicts.trueWording: “my preference is to write a very tight point-of-view... in any given scene, you will only be with one character”
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture, same first/third-person answer. Quote exact. The 'never switching mid-conversation' limb is the next sentence: 'You will not have a conversation where I suddenly switch from my point-of-view, to your point-of-view, and then back.'

verdicts.trueWording: “It is the most intimate voice” — the voice used with families in the evening
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture, same answer. Quote exact. Both similes present: 'It’s the voice we use when we talk to our families in the evening, or when your mom is telling you about what things were when she was a kid.' Claim’s 'a mother recounting her childhood' is the page’s 'your mom is telling you about what things were when she was a kid'.

verdicts.trueWording: “full of pratfalls and silliness, and humour, which is fun but it lessens the impact”
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture, answer on her influences. Quote exact, and the page carries the full 'hurt or disappointed' ending: 'it lessens the impact that you feel if the character is hurt or disappointed.'

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the exclusivity — that ONLY readers attending to every detail would have picked the clues up; the page says 'some readers who were really reading every detail of the book would definitely have picked up that there was more to come', and immediately before that 'a lot of very astute readers picked up on all the clues that were left' and 'I got a lot of emails about that', which asserts no such restriction
verdicts.trueWording: “some readers who were really reading every detail” would definitely have noticed
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture of the Arched Doorway transcript; quote exact in the answer to 'Did you know you’d be coming back all these years later'. The clue-planting limb is supported ('all the clues that were left'; 'There’s even a phrase toward the end where I speak about how the minstrel pauses to catch his breath before he sweeps into the final chorus'). Secondary softness: 'the Tawny Man trilogy' is never named on the page — the referent is the interviewer’s 'you last wrote about Fitz and the Fool in 2003' and Hobb’s 'When I ended it' — correct externally but identified only by context.

verdicts.trueWording: “Her overreliance on adverbs often stunts the novel’s flow”
verdicts.note: fantasy-faction.com fetched live, 200, full review by Lew Kelly dated August 19, 2014. Quote exact, in the 'The opening of the novel' paragraph, which is squarely within the Ship of Magic discussion (Captain Kennit on the beach). The page hedges with 'often'; the claim drops it, which does not change the charge.

verdicts.trueWording: “As their domestic situation worsens, so does the political situation in Bingtown”
verdicts.note: Live fantasy-faction.com. Quote exact, in the Mad Ship paragraph, and the antecedent 'their' is named in the preceding sentence: 'The Bingtown Vestrits’ storyline is much more engaging this second time around.' Household-and-city pairing is exactly what the sentence asserts.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the choice is a HOUSEHOLD one — the page says 'Many of the characters face a choice between a morally correct action or a profitable one', attributing it to characters generally (Kennit, Wintrow and others as well as the Vestrits), never to a household
verdicts.trueWording: “Many of the characters face a choice” between moral and profitable
verdicts.note: Live fantasy-faction.com. Quote exact and the first limb fully supported: 'Hobb’s major theme in the trilogy is morality.' Only the 'household' framing is the claim author’s addition (it matches the chunk’s 'consequence on a household' feature bucket, not the review’s wording).

verdicts.trueWording: “her talent truly shines when she’s deep inside a characters head”
verdicts.note: Live fantasy-faction.com. Quote exact (the page really does print 'a characters head' without the apostrophe). Second limb is on the same page, three paragraphs earlier: 'The viewpoints shift many times across a chapter, and though the characters are well-rounded and realistic, it can be difficult to empathise with them when they feel so distanced.' Only the locator differs — that limb sits in the 'It’s a far more complicated story' paragraph, not the 'opening of the novel' one.

verdicts.trueWording: “convey a great deal of historical, societal, and environmental information... without it sounding explanatory”
verdicts.note: hearwritenow.com fetched live, 200. Quote exact and the whole limb chain is one sentence: 'Hobb is able to convey a great deal of historical, societal, and environmental information through various characters who know different aspects of the same events, without it sounding explanatory.' Locator drift only: it is the second paragraph of the 'The Liveship Traders' section, not the third.

verdicts.trueWording: “opens Liveship Traders up to multiple viewpoints (professionally contained to one viewpoint per scene)”
verdicts.note: Live hearwritenow.com. Quote exact, in the first paragraph of the 'The Liveship Traders' section as stated. Reviewer is Elle Neal ('Review copyright © Elle Neal 2006 Updated 2017, 2021'). Note the same reviewer later complains that 'there are too many variations in viewpoint... and the scenes break far too quickly' — a criticism of frequency, not of the one-viewpoint-per-scene containment, so it does not cut against the claim.
